walkthroughs.body_html:
Socialisation, Culture & Identity — a core area of GCSE Sociology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Socialisation, Culture & Identity brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Socialisation, Culture & Identity.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Early learning of norms and values, primarily within the family.
The most important socialisation, happening in school.
Learning facts in primary school.
Both positivists and interpretivists prefer experiments above all else.

mcqs.q: Why do positivists and interpretivists prefer different methods?
options: Positivists like numbers and interpretivists like words — that's the whole difference.

Positivists treat sociology like natural science, seeking objective measurable patterns — preferring quantitative methods. Interpretivists believe humans construct meaning, requiring qualitative methods to access subjective experience.
Both positivists and interpretivists prefer experiments above all else.
Learning facts in primary school.

mcqs.q: What is a self-fulfilling prophecy in education?
options: When teachers' expectations (often based on labels) influence pupil behaviour and achievement — pupils labelled as 'bright' tend to do better, those labelled 'thick' worse, regardless of underlying ability (Rosenthal and Jacobson).
A self-fulfilling prophecy is when teachers predict the future accurately.
A self-fulfilling prophecy is when a student predicts their own grade correctly.
Learning facts in primary school.
